The State Emergency Management Committee is established by the State Emergency and 
Rescue Management Act 1989.  Included in its functions is to facilitate strategic state level 
emergency management capability through inter -agency coordination, cooperation and 
information sharing arrangements. 
 
The Committee consists of executive members of the NSW emergency service 
organisations, the State Emergency Operations Controller, the State Emergency Recovery 
Controller and senior officers from government agencies with responsibilities for the 
delivery of functional services in an emergency. 
 
The reporting period of 2014 -2015 once again brought about challenges to test the NSW 
emergency arrangements, with severe storms and floods impacting the Hunter, Central 
Coast and Sydney Metropolitan areas of NSW in A pril 2015 and the Martin Place Siege in 
Sydney in December 2014.  
 
The April Storms impacted a number of areas of NSW, and caused significant damage 
including flooding and prolonged power outages across the Hunter and Central Coast 
regions. The two week pe riod in late April into early May resulted in over 21,600 request 
for assistance, making it the biggest storm response in NSW State Emergency Service 
history and one of the most severe event to have impacted these regions in the last decade. 
 
We all know the horrific details of the barbaric behaviour that happened in Martin Place in 
December 2014.  Two innocent people lost their lives that day. The day following the end 
of the Siege a review jointly commissioned by the Prime Minister of Australia and the 
Premier of  New South Wales was announced. The State Emergency Management 
Committee contributed to finalising some of the recommendations in the report. The Joint 
Commonwealth and New South Wales Review report was published in January 2015.  
 
The State Emergency Management Committee undertook a strategic planning session for 
the second time in June 2015.The arrangements in NSW are working well, however, the 
session was conducted to prepare for future challenges and make improvements to ensure 
NSW remains at the forefront of emergency management in Australia.  
 
Despite the significant work that has been achieved and the ongoing work various agencies 
are still involved in, the SEMC progressed other key pieces of work. This included the 
endorsement and publication of the Mine Sub Plan, NSW State Flood Plan, Tsunami 
Emergency Sub Plan and the Sydney and North Sydney CBD Evacuation Management Sub 
Plan as well as finalising the templates and guidelines for the preparation of Local 
Emergency Management Plans.  
 
The State Emergency Management Committee is a vital component of what I believe to be 
Australia’s foremost Emergency Management framework. NSW enjoys the reputation for 
having a well-developed clearly defined emergency response and planning system. I would 
like to thank all Members for their significant contributions during the year.

Fire & Rescue NSW  
 
Fire & Rescue NSW (FRNSW) is r esponsible for all fires within Fire Districts established 
under the Fire Brigades Act 1989 and provides the majority of accredited rescue units in 
NSW. It is the sole Combat Agency for hazardous material emergencies throughout NSW 
and for major structural collapse rescue under the Major Structure Collapse Sub Plan of 
the State Emergency Management Plan. FRNSW is also responsible for the management, 
maintenance and deployment of the NSW Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) Task Force 
within NSW, nationally and in ternationally. The Task Force is accredited by the United 
Nations as a Heavy Rescue Task Force suitable for international deployment following 
earthquakes and other disasters.  FRNSW responds beyond Fire Districts when requested 
to support the NSW Rural Fi re Service (NSWRFS), for example at major bushfires and 
fires involving buildings, and supports other agencies, for example the NSW State 
Emergency Service (NSWSES) at floods and storms, and the Ambulance Service of NSW 
at some medical emergencies.  
 
FRNSW is about the 4th largest urban fire service in the world. There are 338 fire stations 
in major metropolitan areas, regional centres and large towns throughout NSW. They are 
staffed by approximately 3,400 career firefighters and approximately 3,300 retained (on-
call) firefighters who operate a fleet of fire engines, tankers, rescue units, ladder / 
platform units, hazardous materials units, and Hazmat boats. In addition there are around 
6,000 Community Fire Unit volunteers attached to about 600 units established in bushfire 
prone areas of NSW.  
 
In 2014-2015 FRNSW firefighters responded to 128,076 emergency incidents, including 
structure fires, bush and grass fires, rescue incidents, chemical spills, flood and storm 
damage and medical assistance calls. An ana lysis of FRNSW responses over a 10 year 
period showed that there has been a significant increase in the number of “real” 
emergencies attended, a reduction in false alarms, that average time spent at emergency 
scenes has increased, and the number of community engagement / prevention activities 
carried out has significantly increased. Today’s firefighters are more likely to be called 
upon to attend a rescue, chemical spill or storm damage call than a structure fire.  
 
Achievements for 2014-2015 
 
Urban Search & Rescue training and Prop 
In February 2015, a new transportable USAR structural collapse training prop was 
commissioned.  Based on the dimensions of an ISO shipping container, the prop is 
transportable and resettable. It simulates a structural collapse where trainees must locate 
and rescue trapped victims. The prop has been used in skills maintenance sessions and 
received the Patrons Award at the 2015 Good Design Awards. A second transportable prop 
was completed in June, and includes a trench collapse and progressive pancake collapse 
scenario. 
 
Lowest number of Fire Deaths in a calendar year 
The overall number of fire deaths per year is a rolling average over a 6 year period and 
has consistently averaged 21 per year since the introduction of new smoke alarm legislation 
in 2006. With the implementation of FRNSW targeted community engagement programs, 
including “Home Fire Safety Check Program”, “Keep Looking Whilst Cooking” and ‘Winter 
Fire Safety Campaign” a significant reduction in fire deaths in the 2014 calendar year was 
achieved with 11 fire related deaths recorded. This is a 48% reduction against previous 
years. FRNSW believes these targeted programs have been a contributing factor to 
achieving these positive results. Introduction nationally of reduced ig nition propensity 
cigarettes, a FRNSW initiative, is also thought to have been a contributory factor.

Significant Operations/Activities for 2014-2015 
 
This year was a busy but fulfilling operational one for FRNSW, bringing many challenges. 
In April severe storms battered many areas of the State. FRN SW and other emergency 
services immediately swung into action, responding to thousands of incidents and assisting 
with recovery efforts. This was one of our busiest periods on record – between 20 April 
and 23 April, our Communication Centres received 7,107  000 calls and crews responded 
to 3,042 storm-related incidents, including powerlines down, roofs damaged or blown off, 
fallen trees, flooding, fires, rescues and hazmat incidents. 
 
Tropical Cyclone Pam - Vanuatu 
FRNSW’s expertise in disaster management is recognised by the United Nations and is 
regularly called upon. This was demonstrated in March this year when Tropical Cyclone 
Pam swept across Vanuatu’s chain of islands, causing widespread devastation. Emergency 
Management Australia and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade asked FRNSW, as 
the on-call international USAR Task Force, to deploy a medium USAR Task Force to Port 
Vila. In response, 56 emergency services personnel led by FRNSW assisted with the 
disaster relief efforts. The team comprised 45 FRNSW rescue, hazmat and command 
specialists, 6 NSW Ambulance Paramedics, 2 doctors, 2 engineers and 1 Police officer. The 
team completed 50 rapid damage assessments on a range of health, education and 
government buildings that were damaged by Tropical Cyclone Pam. Some of the team's 
work included repairs to the Port Vila Hospital, public schools in and around Port Vila and 
a maternity centre.  
 
Factory fire Smithfield 
On the morning of Saturday 26 March the one of the largest industrial fires for some years 
occurred at Smithfield. A large fire in a car wrecking yard spread to a nearby furniture 
factory then continued to spread to other buildings. A 13th Alarm response saw 42 fire 
appliances and 160 firefighters r espond to the scene, and the Commissioner took charge 
of operations at the height of the fire.  Two yet to be commissioned bulk Compressed Air 
Foam System (CAFS) tankers were deployed with instructors and proved to be decisive. 
The appliances carry 9500 litres of water, 200 litres of class A foam and a remote controlled 
nozzle. They were deployed on either side of a building that was under threat, with the 
CAFS immediately reducing fire intensity.   
 
Chemical fire at a renewable energy solar power plant at Jemalong 
On Saturday 13 June FRNSW firefighters from Condobolin and Forbes responded to a 
chemical fire at a renewable energy solar power plant at Jemalong, about 35 kilometres 
west of Forbes in NSW RFS area. 
 
En-route firefighters were informed of the pre sence of liquid sodium which reacts very 
violently with water. RFS crews already on scene were advised of the danger of using water 
and withdrew to safe positions.  
 
On arrival FRNSW crews found a tank containing 120,000 litres of liquid sodium leaking, 
with the resulting spill igniting on contact with the air.  Soda ash was used to assist in 
smothering the fire with additional supplies having to be sourced from other parts of NSW 
and the ACT. Rain added to the complexity of the operation.  
The incident co ntinued for 5 days until the temperature of the tank could be reduced to 
help solidify the liquid and stop the leak. FRNSW fire and hazmat crews from as far away 
as Culcairn, Young, Dubbo, Temora, Orange, Cowra, Wentworth, Wagga Wagga, Kelso, 
Bathurst and Sydney attended the incident.

STATEMENT (ANNUAL REPORT) 
 
Digital Information Security Annual Attestation Statement for the 2014-
2015 Financial Year for the State Emergency Management Committee 
 
 
 
The State Emergency Management Committee’s secretariat support is provided by the Ministry for 
Police and Emergency Services. The State Emergency Management Committee’s is included in the 
Ministry for Police and Emergency Services information security management system and information 
security policy. 
 
The Ministry for Police and Emergency Services has implemented an information security management 
system and initial security policy based on ISO 27001. A minimum security control baseline based on 
NSW Government Digital Information Security Policy, M2012-15 guidelines has been put in place. 
 
The Ministry had an independent third party review of its Information and Communications Technology 
(ICT) strategy and governance controls in 2014 -2015. Several risks were identified, and th e Ministry 
has been working to address those issues. 
 
I, Phil ip Koperberg, am of the opinion that the State Emergency Management Committee had an 
Information Security Management System in place during the financial year being reported on 
consistent with the Core Requirements set out in the Digital Information Security Policy for the NSW 
Public Sector. 
 
I, Philip Koperberg, am of the opinion that the security controls in place to mitigate many of the 
identified risks to the digital information and digital information systems. 
 
I, Philip Koperberg, am of the opinion that there are no other Public Sector Agencies, or parts thereof, 
under the control of the State Emergency Management Committee with a risk profile sufficient to 
warrant an independent Information Security Management System.  
 
The State Emergency Management Committee has also adopted the NSW Government Information 
Classification and Labelling Guidelines. 
 
The State Emergency Management Committee will continue to address digital information security 
issues as the Ministry is integrated into the Department of Justice in 2015-2016. 
 
 
Each NSW Government Department and Statutory Body must include a Digital Information 
Security Annual Attestation Statement in its Annual Report under the section dealing with risk 
management and insurance activities.
